content: The cookie-cutter shark, scientifically known as Isistius brasiliensis, is a small species of dogfish shark that is rarely observed. It is also referred to as the cigar shark or luminous shark. Anatomy and Morphology Cookie-cutter sharks are capable of emitting a green glow and can grow up to 50 cm (20 inches) in length. The underside of the shark is bioluminescent, producing a pale blue-green light that blends with the ambient light from the ocean's surface. This bioluminescence serves as camouflage, making the shark less visible to creatures below it. However, a small, non-luminous patch on its underside appears dark, creating the illusion of a smaller fish. This deceptive feature lures predatory fish, such as tuna, into attacking what they perceive to be prey. When the predator strikes, the cookie-cutter shark counterattacks, securing its own meal. This is the only known example of a bioluminescent lure being created by the absence of light, contrasting with the light-emitting lures of species like anglerfish. Distribution The cookie-cutter shark is found worldwide in deep oceanic waters. It has been recorded at depths of approximately 1,000 meters (3,300 feet). Ecology and Life History Feeding Ecology The shark derives its name from its unique feeding behavior, which involves removing small, circular plugs of flesh from whales and large fish. It is hypothesized that the shark uses its jaws to latch onto its much larger prey and then rotates its body to create a highly symmetrical wound. This feeding strategy has led to the classification of cookie-cutter sharks as parasitic organisms. Life History Cookie-cutter sharks reproduce via aplacental viviparity, a reproductive method also observed in great white sharks. Beyond this, little is known about their reproductive biology. Etymology and Taxonomic History The name cookie-cutter shark originates from its feeding style, which often leaves perfectly round, cookie-cutter-shaped wounds in the skin of large marine mammals, other sharks, and even the rubber coatings of submarines. Interaction with Humans Human interactions with cookie-cutter sharks are rare. However, one notable incident involved a cookie-cutter shark biting into the rubber sonar dome of a U.S. Navy submarine. This caused damage to the sonar housing and rendered the submarine temporarily inoperable until the rubber coating could be replaced.
